questions.question: Explain what causes the tides and why most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day.
questions.expected_answer: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity. It pulls most strongly on the ocean nearest to it, forming a bulge facing the Moon (high tide); it pulls the Earth more than the water on the far side, leaving a second bulge on the opposite side. Between the bulges the water is lower (low tides). As the Earth rotates once a day, each place passes through both bulges and both low areas, giving two high and two low tides in about 24 hours 50 minutes.

questions.question: Distinguish between spring tides and neap tides, including the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon and the phases at which they occur.
questions.expected_answer: Spring tides: the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line (new Moon and full Moon); the Sun's and Moon's pulls combine, giving the highest high tides and lowest low tides (largest tidal range). Neap tides: the Sun and Moon are at right angles as seen from Earth (first and last quarter); their pulls partly cancel, giving lower high tides and higher low tides (smallest tidal range). Each occurs about every two weeks.

questions.question: Describe the intertidal zone and explain three adaptations that help organisms survive there.
questions.expected_answer: The intertidal zone is the shore between the highest high tide and the lowest low tide; organisms there are covered by sea water and then exposed to air, sun and waves twice a day. Adaptations (any three): limpets clamp tightly to rock with a muscular foot and seal water inside their shells; mussels shut their shells and anchor with strong threads; barnacles close their plates; sea anemones pull in their tentacles to avoid drying out; animals shelter in rock pools; oystercatchers time feeding to low tide.
